hero.headline: Federal judge declines to block Trump executive order limiting mail-in voting
hero.body:
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., has declined to temporarily block President Trump's executive order that restricts mail-in voting. The decision allows the order to remain in effect while legal challenges continue through the courts.

Democrats filed a lawsuit seeking to halt the executive order, arguing that it improperly limits voting access for Americans. The judge's refusal to issue a preliminary injunction represents a setback for those opposing the measure, though the underlying legal questions about the order's validity will continue to be litigated.

The executive order places new restrictions on voting by mail, a practice that has grown significantly in recent elections. Supporters of the restrictions argue they are necessary to ensure election security, while critics contend that the limitations could make it harder for some Americans to vote. Voting rights advocates have expressed particular concern that the changes could disproportionately affect voters who depend on mail-in ballots due to work schedules, disabilities, or other circumstances.

By declining to block the order, the judge has allowed it to take effect as originally planned. However, the lawsuit challenging its legality will continue moving through the courts system. The case may ultimately determine whether the executive order exceeds presidential authority over election procedures.

The ruling highlights ongoing disputes about election administration and the balance of power between federal and state authorities in setting voting rules. Legal experts have noted that the case could eventually shape how mail-in voting is conducted in future elections, depending on how courts ultimately rule on the merits of the legal challenge.

Another judge may also rule on the order soon, according to reports. The decision came after arguments from both sides about the scope of presidential power over election procedures and whether the order complies with existing voting rights laws.

The order's opponents indicated they plan to continue pursuing their legal challenge despite this setback. The case represents a significant development in the broader debate over voting methods and election access that has intensified in recent years.

The ruling was reported by multiple major news outlets including Reuters, NPR, The Hill, Bloomberg, and The New York Times, underscoring the national significance of the decision.

cards.headline: U.S. and Iran exchange strikes as ceasefire negotiations continue
cards.body:
The United States and Iran engaged in direct military conflict late Thursday, marking the most serious test of their month-long ceasefire. The exchange of fire occurred even as diplomats continued working toward a longer-term agreement to end the three-month war.

According to the U.S. military, Iranian forces launched multiple missiles, drones, and small boats at three American destroyers transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. Central Command said no American vessels were struck and that its forces responded by targeting Iranian military facilities responsible for the attacks, including missile and drone launch sites, command centers, and surveillance installations.

Iran disputed the American account. Iran's military said the U.S. violated the ceasefire by attacking an Iranian oil tanker and another ship in the strait. Military officials also accused the U.S. of conducting airstrikes on civilian areas along Iranian coasts, including the island of Qeshm, which is home to approximately 150,000 people and a water desalination plant. Iran claimed its armed forces responded by attacking American military vessels.

President Donald Trump characterized the confrontation differently, calling it a "love tap" during an ABC News interview. "They trifled with us today," Trump said. "We blew them away." He emphasized that no American assets sustained damage and that Iranian attackers and their equipment were "completely destroyed."

Despite the military exchange, both sides signaled reluctance to return to full-scale war. Trump said a negotiated deal "might not happen, but it could happen any day," claiming Iran wanted an agreement more than he did. Iranian officials have indicated openness to talks, though some favor extending negotiations closer to the U.S. midterm elections, when Trump administration pressure to settle may intensify.

Before Thursday's strikes, reports indicated the U.S. and Iran were close to a temporary agreement. Negotiators had reportedly shared a one-page memorandum addressing a potential 60-day truce extension, though the arrangement requires Trump's approval. Regional diplomats suggest Iran could overplay its hand by dragging out talks, as the current moment offers an opportunity to claim victory and end the war.

The U.S. has been enforcing a naval blockade aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz. On Monday, Trump announced "Project Freedom," directing warships to guide stranded tankers through the waterway while protecting them from Iranian interference.

Oil prices initially spiked to around $101 per barrel following reports of the strikes but pulled back after news that an agreement awaited final approval. The fragile ceasefire has now come under significant strain, though neither side appears ready for escalation toward resumed full-scale fighting.

cards.headline: Inflation Rises to Fastest Pace in Nearly Three Years as Iran War Pushes Up Prices
cards.body:
Consumer prices jumped at their fastest rate in nearly three years during April, driven largely by surging energy costs tied to the ongoing conflict with Iran. The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure, climbed 3.8% over the 12-month period, exceeding the central bank's 2% target.

The April inflation report marks the first official reading under new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh. The data reveals that Americans' real purchasing power continues to decline, with disposable income falling 0.5% after adjusting for inflation in April. This represents the third consecutive monthly drop in household income when accounting for price increases.

The war with Iran has significantly disrupted global energy markets and supply chains. The conflict has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and strained access to goods including fertilizers, aluminum, and consumer products. Gasoline prices have surged more than 50% since the conflict began in late February, with the national average retail price shooting up 12.3% in April alone.

Beyond energy, inflation pressures are spreading across the economy. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, rose to 3.3% year-over-year in April. Food prices rebounded 0.5%, while services prices increased 0.3% for the third straight month. Housing and utilities costs climbed 0.6%.

The inflation surge comes as consumer spending weakens. Real consumer spending edged up just 0.1% in April after increasing 0.3% in March. The government also revised down first-quarter GDP growth to 1.6% from the previously reported 2.0%, while cutting consumer spending growth from 1.6% to 1.4%.

Households are depleting savings to maintain spending levels despite rising prices. The savings rate dropped to 2.6% in April, the lowest level since June 2022, down from 3.2% in March. Tax refunds have provided some cushion for lower-income families, but economists expect consumers will eventually pull back and attempt to rebuild savings.

The inflation pressure threatens both the Fed's credibility and Trump's political standing. Trump won the 2024 election partly on promises to lower inflation, but rising prices have eroded his approval rating, particularly among Republicans. The issue poses risks to the Republican party's congressional majority ahead of midterm elections.

Financial markets are watching for the Fed's response. Current expectations suggest the central bank will maintain interest rates in the 3.50% to 3.75% range well into 2027. However, minutes from recent Fed meetings show a growing number of policymakers are open to rate hikes, setting up potential conflict with the White House, which has continued pressuring the Fed to cut rates.

cards.headline: US and Iran reach tentative deal to extend ceasefire, reopen Strait of Hormuz
cards.body:
The United States and Iran have reached a tentative agreement to extend their ceasefire for 60 days and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to U.S. sources. The deal requires approval from President Trump before it can take effect.

The memorandum of understanding would establish terms for maintaining the ceasefire over the next two months. During this period, the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened to restore a vital shipping route for global oil transport. The waterway has been largely closed since the conflict began, contributing to energy price increases that have affected household budgets worldwide.

Under the proposed agreement, Iran would be permitted to freely sell oil and would clear mines it deployed in the strait. Iran would also agree not to impose tolls on ships using the waterway. In return, the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports that has been in place since April 13. Additionally, some Iranian assets held in foreign banks would reportedly be unfrozen.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the deal could achieve "a completely open" Strait of Hormuz "without tolls" if successful. However, Iranian media reported that the strait would remain under Iranian control.

The agreement would also include talks on limiting Iran's nuclear program during the 60-day period. Hostilities would reportedly be halted on all fronts, including Israeli operations and the conflict involving Lebanon.

A senior Iranian source told Reuters that Tehran had not agreed to surrender its highly enriched uranium stockpile as part of the preliminary agreement. The source indicated that Iran's nuclear issue was not included in these initial talks, contradicting earlier reports that Tehran had expressed willingness to give up such material.

The agreement notably does not appear to address Iran's ballistic missile program or constraints on Iran's support for regional allies including Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen.

The tentative nature of the deal means its implementation remains uncertain. Trump's approval is necessary before the arrangement becomes operational. While negotiations continue, recent military activity has occurred, with the U.S. reportedly striking Iranian targets and prompting an apparent Iranian retaliatory attack on an American airbase in Kuwait.

The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz represents a significant development in restoring international commerce. The waterway handles a substantial portion of the world's oil supply, and its closure has been a major factor driving up energy prices. Oil markets responded positively to reports of the breakthrough, with global oil prices falling following news of the tentative agreement.

cards.headline: Illinois passes AI safety law as Anthropic and OpenAI support testing requirements
cards.teaser: The state enacted legislation requiring safety testing for AI systems, with support from major AI companies.
cards.body:
Illinois passed a law requiring safety testing for artificial intelligence systems. The legislation represents a shift in AI regulation at the state level.

Anthropic and OpenAI both supported the testing requirements included in the law. The state-level action comes as federal AI regulation remains limited.

cards.headline: Canadian prime minister calls for new U.S. relationship
cards.teaser: Mark Carney said Canada's distancing from the United States benefits both nations.
cards.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke in New York about recalibrating the bilateral relationship between Canada and the United States. He argued that Canada's move toward greater distance from the U.S. benefits both nations.

The remarks signal a shift in how Canada is positioning itself relative to its neighbor.

cards.headline: Justice Department sues four states over denied undercover plates for immigration officers
cards.teaser: The DOJ filed lawsuits against Maine, Washington, Oregon and Massachusetts for refusing to issue confidential license plates to federal immigration agents.
cards.body:
The Department of Justice filed lawsuits Thursday against Maine, Washington, Oregon and Massachusetts for refusing to issue undercover license plates to federal immigration officers. The legal action followed a DOJ letter sent earlier in the month requesting that all four states provide confidential plates for federal agents conducting enforcement operations.

The states had declined to issue the special plates, prompting the federal government to pursue legal action to compel compliance.

cards.headline: Israel conducts targeted strike in Beirut
cards.teaser: The Lebanese capital had largely been spared in recent fighting between Israel and Hezbollah.
cards.body:
Israel carried out a targeted strike in Beirut, marking a significant escalation in the conflict with Hezbollah. The Lebanese capital had previously been largely spared despite both sides accusing each other of violating the ceasefire agreement reached last month.

The strike represents a notable shift in the pattern of recent hostilities, as Beirut itself had not been targeted in the ongoing tensions between Israel and Hezbollah.

cards.headline: Gaza strike kills children, targets Hamas commander
cards.teaser: Hospitals in Gaza City reported multiple casualties from an Israeli strike.
cards.body:
An Israeli strike on Gaza City killed at least five children, according to local hospitals. The operation targeted a Hamas commander.

Hamas confirmed that Mohammed Odeh, the head of its military wing, was killed in the strike on a residential building along with his wife and two children.

cards.headline: 16 students die in Kenya school fire
cards.teaser: Parents waited for news of their children roughly 12 hours after the fire.
cards.body:
At least 16 students have died in a fire at Utumishi girls academy in Gilgil, Nakuru county, in Kenya's Rift Valley. The blaze broke out just after midnight at the school's dormitory, located approximately 76 miles north-west of Nairobi.

Many parents were still waiting for updates on their children about 12 hours after the fire. The incident has renewed concerns about safety standards at Kenyan schools, following previous fires at educational facilities in the country.

cards.headline: Justice Department opens criminal investigation into Trump accuser
cards.teaser: The probe centers on whether E Jean Carroll lied about funding for her civil lawsuit.
cards.body:
The U.S. Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into E. Jean Carroll, the former columnist who won civil lawsuits against President Donald Trump. Investigators are examining whether Carroll made false statements regarding the funding sources for her civil case against Trump.

Carroll's civil lawsuits against Trump resulted in court victories prior to his return to the presidency. The criminal probe marks a significant new development in their ongoing legal disputes.

cards.headline: Spanish prime minister faces mounting pressure to resign
cards.teaser: A judge accused Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's party of corruption after police searched party offices.
cards.body:
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain faced mounting calls to resign after a judge accused his party of corruption. Police searched his party's offices as part of the investigation.

The corruption accusations and subsequent police search have intensified political pressure on Sánchez. Opposition parties and critics have called for his resignation in response to the judicial proceedings against his party.

cards.headline: Three injured in Swiss train station stabbing
cards.teaser: A 31-year-old Swiss man was arrested following the incident.
cards.body:
Three people were injured in a stabbing at a Swiss train station. Police arrested a 31-year-old Swiss man in connection with the incident.

Images from the scene showed parts of the station cordoned off following the attack.

cards.headline: Supreme Court rules for Mississippi death row inmate in racial bias case
cards.teaser: The court sided with a Mississippi man on death row in a case involving allegations of racial bias.
cards.body:
The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in favor of Terry Pitchford, a Black man on death row in Mississippi, who challenged his capital murder conviction on grounds of racial bias. Pitchford was 18 when convicted and argued that Black jurors were improperly excluded from his trial.

The decision represents a significant legal victory for Pitchford and could influence how his case proceeds in lower courts as it moves forward.

cards.headline: Trump refiles $10 billion defamation lawsuit against Wall Street Journal
cards.teaser: President Trump has refiled a defamation lawsuit seeking $10 billion in damages from the Wall Street Journal's publisher.
cards.body:
President Trump has refiled a $10 billion defamation lawsuit against Dow Jones, the publisher of the Wall Street Journal, after a Florida judge dismissed the original case last month. The lawsuit centers on a Wall Street Journal article alleging that Trump sent a "bawdy" letter to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003.

Trump's legal team claims the newspaper article damaged his reputation by describing a card bearing his signature. The case represents a significant legal battle pitting the U.S. president against Rupert Murdoch, a key media ally.

cards.headline: US and Iran exchange strikes during fragile ceasefire
cards.teaser: Iran says it targeted an American base following fresh US strikes, testing a ceasefire between the two nations.
cards.body:
Iran announced it targeted an American military base following fresh US strikes. The exchange occurred amid ongoing negotiations to resolve a three-month conflict between the two nations.

Despite the latest military exchange, neither side appears interested in returning to full-scale warfare. The ceasefire remains fragile as diplomatic efforts continue to establish a lasting peace agreement.

cards.headline: Man dies after escaping police vehicle on way to court
cards.teaser: A man was killed by a train in Hertfordshire after escaping from a vehicle transporting him to court.
cards.body:
A man died after being struck by a train in Hertfordshire following his escape from a vehicle that was transporting him to court. The incident occurred while he was in police custody.

Hertfordshire Police referred the case to the Independent Office for Police Conduct, the agency responsible for overseeing investigations into incidents involving law enforcement. The referral is standard procedure for deaths that occur during or following police contact.

cards.headline: Two boys die in separate water incidents during heatwave
cards.teaser: A boy's body was recovered from a pond in Kent, and a teen died in the River Thames in Oxford.
cards.body:
A boy's body was recovered from a pond in Kent, and a teenager died in the River Thames in Oxford. These deaths occurred during the latest heatwave affecting the region.

The incidents represent recent water-related fatalities during a period of hot weather.

cards.headline: Australian woman charged with traveling to Syria to join Islamic State
cards.teaser: An Australian woman faces charges for allegedly traveling to Syria to join the Islamic State terror group.
cards.body:
Australian authorities charged a woman with traveling to Syria to join the Islamic State. The arrest occurred eight months after she returned to Australia from Lebanon with her children.

The charges relate to her alleged travel to Syria for the purpose of joining the terrorist organization. She had been living in Lebanon before returning to Australia with her children prior to her arrest.

cards.headline: Caesars Entertainment Sold to Fertitta Entertainment for $17.6 Billion
cards.teaser: Hospitality executive Tilman Fertitta has agreed to acquire the casino operator in one of the largest gaming industry deals.
cards.body:
Caesars Entertainment has been sold to Fertitta Entertainment in a deal valued at $17.6 billion to $18 billion. The acquisition price includes $5.7 billion for the company itself, with the combined entity controlling four Atlantic City casinos.

Tilman Fertitta, owner of the Houston Rockets and a known associate of President Trump, is expanding his leisure and hospitality holdings with the purchase. Bond prices for Caesars fell following announcement of the takeover. The deal represents a major consolidation in the casino and entertainment industry.

cards.headline: Google Employee Charged With Using Inside Search Data to Make $1.2 Million on Polymarket
cards.teaser: Federal prosecutors charged the engineer with using confidential company information to rig bets on the prediction market platform.
cards.body:
Michele Spagnuolo, a 36-year-old Italian software engineer at Google, has been charged by the Department of Justice with using insider information to place bets on Polymarket. According to unsealed court documents, Spagnuolo earned $1.2 million in profits by wagering on outcomes related to Google's Year in Search campaign, risking over $2.7 million in total bets.

The case represents an escalating concern about insider trading in prediction markets. Spagnuolo allegedly leveraged confidential access to Google search data to gain unfair advantages when betting on long-shot outcomes. His arrest follows a similar prosecution one month earlier involving a US Army soldier accused of using classified military information for Polymarket wagers.

cards.headline: European Union Fines Temu 200 Million Euros for Allowing Illegal Product Sales
cards.teaser: The European Commission penalized the Chinese-owned online retailer for failing to address risks from unsafe goods sold on its platform.
cards.body:
The European Commission has fined Temu €200 million for failing to prevent the sale of illegal and dangerous products on its platform. Following a 19-month investigation, regulators found that consumers shopping on the Chinese website were very likely to encounter unsafe items, including baby toys and faulty electronics.

The penalty reflects growing EU enforcement action against online marketplaces, particularly those based outside the bloc. European regulators are increasing scrutiny of e-commerce platforms over consumer protection and product safety concerns.

cards.headline: Trump Refiles $10 Billion Defamation Lawsuit Against Wall Street Journal
cards.teaser: The president has submitted a new version of his suit after a judge dismissed an earlier filing related to coverage of a note to Jeffrey Epstein.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump's legal team has refiled a $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal after a Florida judge dismissed the earlier version last month. The case centers on a Wall Street Journal article about a letter Trump allegedly sent to Jeffrey Epstein in 2003, which the newspaper described as "bawdy."

The refiled suit represents a significant legal dispute between Trump and Rupert Murdoch, who owns the Journal. Trump's legal team claims the newspaper's reporting damaged his reputation through its characterization of the correspondence with the disgraced financier.

cards.headline: Bari Weiss Appoints Nick Bilton to Lead CBS's 60 Minutes
cards.teaser: The tech journalist and filmmaker will take over the program as part of an overhaul that included firing correspondent Cecilia Vega.
cards.body:
Nick Bilton, a technology journalist and filmmaker, has been named to lead CBS's 60 Minutes by network editor in chief Bari Weiss. Bilton said he plans to bring new voices to the long-running news program.

The appointment is part of a broader restructuring at CBS under Weiss. The changes included the dismissal of correspondent Cecilia Vega from the show. Bilton's background in technology journalism marks a shift in leadership for the program, which has traditionally been helmed by broadcast news veterans.

cards.headline: Youth Unemployment Expected to Reach 1.25 Million by 2031, Report Warns
cards.teaser: A major study cautions that opportunities are shrinking for young people, with the number out of work, education or training set to rise sharply.
cards.body:
The number of 16 to 24-year-olds not in work, education or training is projected to reach 1.25 million by 2031, according to a new report. The study warns that opportunities are diminishing for young people across the economy.

hero.headline: U.S. says troops were targeted with location data as senator warns ad industry poses national security threat
hero.body:
U.S. military personnel have been targeted using location data collected and sold through commercial channels, according to government statements that have prompted lawmakers to raise alarm about the advertising technology industry's national security implications.

The disclosure highlights a growing vulnerability in how personal location information flows through the commercial data marketplace. Advertising technology companies routinely collect location data from smartphones and other connected devices, then package and sell this information to data brokers and other buyers. This data can reveal detailed patterns about where individuals live, work, and travel.

Military personnel who carry personal devices face particular risks. Applications installed on these devices can share location information with advertising networks without users fully understanding how that data will be used or who might eventually access it. Once location data enters the commercial data broker market, it becomes difficult for consumers to track or control its distribution.

The concern is especially acute because precise location information can expose sensitive details when connected to other databases. Knowing where someone travels regularly can reveal their home, workplace, school, or place of worship. For military personnel, this information could theoretically be purchased by foreign adversaries or other actors seeking to understand troop movements or deployment patterns near military installations.

Security researchers have repeatedly demonstrated that location data described as anonymized or aggregated can be re-identified to track specific individuals. Despite these findings, the commercial data collection industry continues to expand, with companies collecting information through vehicles, apps, and other connected devices.

The statement about troops being targeted comes as lawmakers intensify scrutiny of the broader data collection ecosystem. A leading privacy advocate in Congress called for treating the advertising technology industry as a national security threat, suggesting that legislative action may follow. Previous attempts to restrict commercial data collection through privacy legislation have stalled, but the national security angle could shift the political dynamics.

The case highlights how commercial data practices create risks that extend beyond consumer privacy concerns. Industries from automotive to advertising have faced increasing pressure over their data handling practices. General Motors recently agreed to pay 12.75 million dollars to settle claims that it sold location and driving data from California consumers to data brokers without proper consent.

The government statement did not specify how many troops were targeted, which military units were affected, or whether the targeting led to actual security breaches. It also did not identify which foreign actors or adversaries may have purchased or accessed the location data.

As commercial data collection becomes more sophisticated and widespread, the tension between industry practices and national security grows sharper. The disclosure about military personnel suggests policymakers are beginning to view data broker regulation not primarily as a consumer privacy issue, but as a military and intelligence concern.

cards.body:
Illinois passed a law requiring safety testing for artificial intelligence systems. The legislation represents a shift in AI regulation at the state level.

Anthropic and OpenAI both supported the testing requirements included in the law. The state-level action comes as federal AI regulation remains limited.

cards.headline: Anthropic releases Opus 4.8 with tool for coordinating multiple AI agents
cards.teaser: The company's new model includes Dynamic Workflows, a feature designed to manage groups of subagents.
cards.body: Dynamic Workflows allows for coordinating swarms of subagents. The tool represents Anthropic's approach to managing multiple AI agents working together on complex tasks.

cards.headline: Waymo launches Chinese-made robotaxi and begins accepting riders
cards.teaser: The company deployed its new Ojai minivan robotaxi after years of development and testing.
cards.body:
Waymo is now accepting passengers in the Ojai, its new Chinese-manufactured robotaxi based on the Zeekr RT minivan. The company is initially offering rides to select passengers in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Phoenix, with plans to gradually expand to additional riders and cities. Initial trips are being offered for free.

The launch comes after several months of testing and represents a significant step forward for Waymo's robotaxi service. The new vehicle is designed to help the company generate revenue as it continues to develop its autonomous driving technology.

cards.headline: Steam Deck sells out in North America after price increase of more than 40 percent
cards.teaser: Valve's handheld gaming device sold out within 24 hours of a substantial price hike, though availability continues in other regions.
cards.body:
The Steam Deck sold out in North America within 24 hours of Valve announcing a price increase exceeding 40 percent. Valve attributed the hike to rising component costs, though the device itself remained unchanged.

The handheld console is still available for purchase in Europe, Australia, and Asia. Valve had previously kept the Steam Deck out of stock for an extended period before relaunching it at the higher price point.

cards.headline: Musk describes Anthropic compute deal as short-term despite SpaceX filing showing payments through 2029
cards.teaser: The xAI founder publicly reframed his company's agreement with Anthropic as cancellable, contradicting SpaceX's regulatory disclosure.
cards.body:
Elon Musk has publicly characterized xAI's compute deal with Anthropic as short-term and cancellable. However, SpaceX's S-1 filing describes the arrangement differently, listing payments extending through May 2029.

The conflicting characterizations—Musk's public statements versus SpaceX's regulatory filing—create a notable discrepancy about the deal's actual terms and duration.

cards.headline: Rivian faces investigation over rear suspension failures on R1 vehicles
cards.teaser: At least two owners lost control after a suspension component broke, both following previous service work.
cards.body:
Rivian is under investigation following rear suspension failures affecting its R1 models. At least two owners experienced loss of control after a critical suspension component broke on their vehicles.

Both incidents involved vehicles that had undergone previous service. Investigators will determine whether the failures stem from manufacturing defects or issues related to service procedures.

hero.headline: TT competitor dies in qualifying crash on Isle of Man
hero.body:
Daniel Ingham, 33, died in a crash during qualifying for the Isle of Man TT on Wednesday. The incident occurred as competitors prepared for the annual motorcycle race on the island's public road course.

The Isle of Man TT is one of the most dangerous motorsport events in the world, held annually on a 37-mile course of closed public roads. Riders compete at speeds exceeding 200 miles per hour through towns, over mountains, and past stone walls with minimal safety barriers.

Ingham's death marks another fatality in the history of the race, which has claimed more than 260 lives since its inception in 1907. The event attracts top motorcycle racers from around the world despite its well-documented risks.

Qualifying sessions allow riders to familiarize themselves with the course and set lap times that determine their starting positions for the main races. These practice runs are often as dangerous as the races themselves, with riders pushing their machines to the limit on unfamiliar sections of the course.

The TT races are scheduled to continue despite the fatal crash. Organizers typically pause briefly to investigate incidents but resume racing after safety reviews. The event draws tens of thousands of spectators to the island each year and represents a significant part of the local economy.

Ingham was competing in his qualifying session when the crash occurred. No additional details about the circumstances of the accident have been released. Race officials conduct investigations after fatal incidents to determine contributing factors and assess whether course modifications are needed.

The Isle of Man, a self-governing British Crown dependency, closes its roads for two weeks each year to host the TT. The race has continued for more than a century despite mounting safety concerns and periodic calls for its cancellation. Supporters argue that competitors participate willingly and understand the risks involved in one of motorsport's most challenging events.

cards.headline: World number one Jannik Sinner eliminated from French Open in second round
cards.teaser: Top-ranked tennis player Jannik Sinner lost to Juan Manuel Cerundolo in five sets at Roland Garros.
cards.body:
World No. 1 Jannik Sinner has been knocked out of the French Open in the second round, losing to Juan Manuel Cerundolo in a five-set match. The Italian star was hampered by an injury during the contest, which proved decisive in his defeat.

The upset ends Sinner's bid for a maiden French Open title and delays his hopes of completing a career Grand Slam at Roland Garros. The result significantly reshapes the men's singles draw as the tournament continues.

cards.headline: Frenchman Paul Magnier wins third stage at Giro d'Italia
cards.teaser: Paul Magnier won stage 18 of the Giro d'Italia in a bunch sprint, securing his third victory of the race.
cards.body:
The 22-year-old French cyclist Paul Magnier claimed his third stage victory at this year's Giro d'Italia by winning stage 18 in a bunch sprint finish at Pieve di Soligo. Magnier, riding for Soudal Quick-Step, was expertly positioned by teammate Jasper Stuyven in the final high-speed turns before powering across the line ahead of two Italian sprinters after 171km of racing.

The hat-trick of victories cements Magnier's status as one of the race's most formidable sprinters, showcasing his consistency in finishing stages at one of cycling's Grand Tours.

cards.headline: Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart addresses team after Trump event appearance
cards.teaser: Jaxson Dart spoke to his Giants teammates following controversy over his appearance at a Donald Trump political event.
cards.body:
New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart addressed his teammates after appearing at a Donald Trump political rally. The appearance generated controversy and prompted Dart to meet with players in the locker room.

Dart was introduced at the Trump event, which led to questions about mixing politics with professional sports. Multiple sources confirmed that Dart spoke with his Giants teammates following the incident. The situation has drawn attention to athlete involvement in political campaigns and how it affects team dynamics.

cards.headline: Vikings quarterbacks Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy discuss competition
cards.teaser: Kyler Murray said his relationship with fellow Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy has been positive during offseason workouts.
cards.body:
Minnesota Vikings quarterbacks Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy addressed their ongoing competition for the starting position during organized team activities. Murray stated that his relationship with McCarthy has been positive as both players work through the offseason program.

McCarthy said there is no awkwardness between the two quarterbacks despite competing for the same role. Both players have been participating in team drills and distributing footballs during OTA sessions as the Vikings coaching staff evaluates the quarterback position ahead of the regular season.

cards.headline: Ronda Rousey responds to Holly Holm rematch proposal
cards.teaser: Former UFC fighter Ronda Rousey said she would defeat Holly Holm in a rematch but maintains she is retired from competition.
cards.body:
Ronda Rousey addressed Holly Holm's request for a rematch, claiming she would defeat Holm if they fought again. Despite her confidence, Rousey emphasized that she remains retired from competitive fighting and has no plans to return to the sport.

Holm knocked out Rousey in 2015, ending Rousey's undefeated record and her UFC bantamweight championship reign. The pair have exchanged comments about a potential rematch, though Rousey has consistently maintained her retirement stance.

cards.headline: Arsenal co-chair credits Covid era for manager's rebuild success
cards.teaser: Josh Kroenke said behind-closed-doors football during the pandemic gave Mikel Arteta space to revive Arsenal.
cards.body:
Arsenal co-chair Josh Kroenke has credited the Covid-19 pandemic period with giving manager Mikel Arteta the opportunity to rebuild the club. Kroenke described Arsenal as a "sleeping giant" that benefited from the unique environment of behind-closed-doors football during lockdown restrictions.

Arteta took charge of Arsenal in late 2019 and led the team through the pandemic era when stadiums were closed to supporters, a period that Kroenke believes provided crucial space for the manager's revival project.

hero.headline: CBS News Removes 60 Minutes Executive Producer and Two Correspondents
hero.body:
CBS News has undergone a significant leadership shake-up at its flagship newsmagazine 60 Minutes. Editor-in-chief Bari Weiss removed executive producers Tanya Simon and Draggan Mihailoivich, along with correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega. Nick Bilton, a former technology columnist, was named to lead the program.

The departures mark a major restructuring at the television industry's most-watched newsmagazine. Simon and Mihailoivich held the two most senior executive producer positions at the show.

Alfonsi's departure came after her contract expired and was not renewed for the show's 59th season. She accused CBS News of penalizing her for refusing to compromise factually accurate reporting. "This was not a routine corporate transition; it was a deliberate choice to penalize a journalist for refusing to sanitize factually accurate reporting, and it sends a chilling message to the entire newsroom," Alfonsi wrote in a statement.

Alfonsi's exit followed an editorial dispute over a segment she reported about a notorious prison in El Salvador. Weiss shelved the story, which sparked national controversy. After the segment was killed, Alfonsi had not appeared on the final three episodes of the show's 58th season.

The correspondent expressed concern about the direction of CBS News operations. "The wall between editorial independence and corporate interest at CBS is being methodically torn down. Journalists willing to challenge authority are being pushed aside in favor of those who will not," Alfonsi said. She also raised questions about editorial decision-making, noting that some executives ask "Is it good for business?" rather than "Is the story true?"

In a public speech last month, Alfonsi decried "the spread of corporate meddling and editorial fear" at CBS News. She warned about the industry's fears of offending powerful interests and losing access to sources, saying journalists should instead fear silence.

The restructuring also affects veteran correspondent Anderson Cooper, who opted to leave 60 Minutes. Cooper emphasized that "the independence of 60 Minutes has been critical" and expressed hope that the program remains true to its core mission. "There are very few things that have been around for as long as 60 Minutes has and maintained the quality that it has," he said.

Bilton brings a background in technology and digital media journalism to his new executive producer role at CBS News. His appointment represents a notable shift in leadership for the program that has maintained its position as a prominent fixture in broadcast journalism for decades.

CBS News has not announced replacements for the correspondent positions vacated by Alfonsi and Vega. The program typically features multiple segments per episode, relying on in-depth interviews and investigative reporting across politics, culture, and other topics.

cards.headline: HBO and A24 Developing Angel Heart Series With Zac Efron
cards.teaser: Zac Efron will star in and executive produce a drama series based on the 1978 horror novel Falling Angel.
cards.body:
HBO and A24 are developing a one-hour drama series based on the 1978 horror novel Falling Angel. Zac Efron will star in and executive produce the project.

Writer Zach Baylin will pen the series and serve as executive producer. Baylin previously created the series Black Rabbit. The novel Falling Angel was adapted into the 1987 film Angel Heart, which starred Mickey Rourke and Robert De Niro.

cards.headline: Chrissy Metz to Join Broadway Cast of & Juliet
cards.teaser: The actress will play Anglique in the jukebox musical for a limited run starting in June.
cards.body:
Chrissy Metz will make her Broadway debut in the jukebox musical & Juliet. She will join the cast as Anglique for a limited run from June 18 through September 13.

Metz is known for playing Kate Pearson on the NBC television show This Is Us. Her character had professional singing ambitions, which required Metz to perform musical numbers on the series.

cards.headline: UTA Signs Outdoor Lifestyle Creator Steven Rinella and MeatEater
cards.teaser: The agency will represent the influential creator and his multiplatform media company.
cards.body:
UTA has signed Steven Rinella and his outdoor lifestyle media company MeatEater for representation. Rinella is a creator in the outdoor lifestyle space.

MeatEater was founded in 1999 and has expanded into a multiplatform company. The business spans video production, podcasts, publishing, commerce, and live events.

cards.headline: NBC News Anchor Hallie Jackson to Expand Linear TV Presence
cards.teaser: The Washington-based anchor will increase her role across NBC News platforms starting next week.
cards.body:
Hallie Jackson will expand her presence on NBC News linear television. The Washington-based anchor currently leads a two-hour program, Hallie Jackson Now, that streams live on the NBC News Now service on most weekdays. She also anchors NBC Nightly News on Sundays.

Starting next week, Jackson will take on additional responsibilities. NBC News is expanding its streaming efforts into traditional television programming.

cards.headline: Four Women Elected to Women In Film Board of Directors
cards.teaser: Tessa Thompson, Katie Aselton, Amy Baer, and Raamla Mohamed Hunter will join the Los Angeles organization's board.
cards.body:
Women In Film, Los Angeles has elected four new members to its 2026 Board of Directors. Actress and producer Tessa Thompson, actress and director Katie Aselton, film producer Amy Baer, and television writer and showrunner Raamla Mohamed Hunter will join the board.

The new directors will work with WIF CEO Kirsten Schaffer and the full board under Board President. Women In Film focuses on advocacy and support for women in the entertainment industry.

cards.headline: Media Access Awards Rebrands as Easterseals Disability Arts & Culture Awards
cards.teaser: The awards honoring disability representation in media will now be called the Darcys.
cards.body:
The Media Access Awards have rebranded as The Easterseals Disability Arts & Culture Awards, known as the Darcys. The awards honor disability representation and authentic filmmaking in media.

Easterseals Disability Services leads the initiative alongside disability community leaders, with Film Independent serving as co-producer. Norman Lear originally founded the awards in 1979.

hero.headline: US and Iran reach tentative deal to extend ceasefire, reopen Strait of Hormuz
hero.body:
The United States and Iran have reached a tentative agreement to extend their ceasefire for 60 days and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to U.S. sources. The deal requires approval from President Trump before it can take effect.

The memorandum of understanding would establish terms for maintaining the ceasefire over the next two months. During this period, the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened to restore a vital shipping route for global oil transport. The waterway has been largely closed since the conflict began, contributing to energy price increases that have affected household budgets worldwide.

Under the proposed agreement, Iran would be permitted to freely sell oil and would clear mines it deployed in the strait. Iran would also agree not to impose tolls on ships using the waterway. In return, the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports that has been in place since April 13. Additionally, some Iranian assets held in foreign banks would reportedly be unfrozen.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the deal could achieve "a completely open" Strait of Hormuz "without tolls" if successful. However, Iranian media reported that the strait would remain under Iranian control.

The agreement would also include talks on limiting Iran's nuclear program during the 60-day period. Hostilities would reportedly be halted on all fronts, including Israeli operations and the conflict involving Lebanon.

A senior Iranian source told Reuters that Tehran had not agreed to surrender its highly enriched uranium stockpile as part of the preliminary agreement. The source indicated that Iran's nuclear issue was not included in these initial talks, contradicting earlier reports that Tehran had expressed willingness to give up such material.

The agreement notably does not appear to address Iran's ballistic missile program or constraints on Iran's support for regional allies including Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen.

The tentative nature of the deal means its implementation remains uncertain. Trump's approval is necessary before the arrangement becomes operational. While negotiations continue, recent military activity has occurred, with the U.S. reportedly striking Iranian targets and prompting an apparent Iranian retaliatory attack on an American airbase in Kuwait.

The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz represents a significant development in restoring international commerce. The waterway handles a substantial portion of the world's oil supply, and its closure has been a major factor driving up energy prices. Oil markets responded positively to reports of the breakthrough, with global oil prices falling following news of the tentative agreement.

cards.headline: Justice Department sues four states over denied undercover plates for immigration officers
cards.teaser: The DOJ filed lawsuits against Maine, Washington, Oregon and Massachusetts for refusing to issue confidential license plates to federal immigration agents.
cards.body:
The Department of Justice filed lawsuits Thursday against Maine, Washington, Oregon and Massachusetts for refusing to issue undercover license plates to federal immigration officers. The legal action followed a DOJ letter sent earlier in the month requesting that all four states provide confidential plates for federal agents conducting enforcement operations.

The states had declined to issue the special plates, prompting the federal government to pursue legal action to compel compliance.

cards.headline: Consumer spending outpaces income growth as households draw down savings
cards.teaser: Americans are spending faster than their income is growing, drawing down savings to support purchases as energy prices rise from the Iran war.
cards.body:
Americans are burning through their financial cushion at an accelerating pace, with spending growth outpacing income growth, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis data. The energy shock from the Iran war has put pressure on household budgets.

Consumer spending has held up despite rock-bottom sentiment readings. New evidence suggests households are increasingly drawing down savings to maintain their spending levels, creating what analysts describe as a fragile dynamic for the broader economy.

cards.headline: California governor announces 100 percent tax on anti-weaponization fund recipients
cards.teaser: Gov. Gavin Newsom said he will impose a 100 percent tax on state residents who receive money from the Trump administration's $1.8 billion fund.
cards.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he will impose a 100 percent tax on state residents who receive payments from the Trump administration's $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization fund." The move is designed to prevent the federal program from benefiting California residents.

The Department of Justice created the fund to compensate alleged victims of what it calls "lawfare and weaponization." The initiative has drawn criticism from a bipartisan group of 35 former federal judges, who filed a lawsuit challenging the fund as a means to direct taxpayer dollars to the president's political allies.

cards.headline: Pentagon appoints venture capitalist accused of anti-Islam remarks to tech board
cards.teaser: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth named Shaun Maguire to a new technology board despite accusations of Islamophobic remarks targeting New York City's mayor.
cards.body:
The Defense Department appointed Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, to its newly established Science, Technology and Innovation Board. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth named Maguire along with 32 other appointees.

Maguire, a Silicon Valley venture capitalist, has been accused of making Islamophobic remarks targeting New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The appointment to the Pentagon technology board comes despite these accusations.

cards.headline: Charlie Kirk settlements reach at least $2 million after employee firings
cards.teaser: At least $2 million in settlements has been agreed to after employees and critics were fired or penalized over their posts about Charlie Kirk following his killing.
cards.body:
At least $2 million in settlements has been agreed to after employees and other critics were fired or penalized over their posts about Charlie Kirk following his killing. The settlements illustrate the limits employers face in regulating workers' political speech.

Kirk's death became a catalyst for a free speech debate after an estimated 600 individuals were fired or punished for criticizing the conservative political activist or downplaying his death. The Trump administration backed the repercussions against those who made critical posts.

cards.headline: NYC Mayor Mamdani creates Commission on Government Efficiency
cards.teaser: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a new commission focused on improving the effectiveness of city government.
cards.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the appointment of a new commission on Thursday focused on improving the effectiveness of the city's government. The Commission on Government Efficiency drew immediate comparisons to the Department of Government Efficiency championed by President Trump and Elon Musk.

The newly unveiled commission, abbreviated as COGE, has a similar name to DOGE, which cut hundreds of thousands of positions. Mamdani's commission will focus on making New York City government more effective.
